title: Talking about the Future of AI in Law with David Wakeling
author: Richard Lichtenstein (interview w/ David Wakeling)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Wakeling does not endorse the proposition that automation is weakening succession routes. He redirects attention to continued junior hiring and to AI implementation as a substantial new source of developmental work, arguing for a changing legal skill mix rather than necessarily fewer lawyers. This complements the cluster’s broader-careers theme but challenges its pipeline framing.
qs: And our juniors in my group, I’m still hiring junior lawyers, and they’re very busy and that’s what they’re doing.
So I think it’s gonna be not stark, it’s gonna be a changing skillset, which might, not mean fewer people frankly, but different kinds of people.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the infrastructure and operating-model thesis and extends it with a concrete law-firm case: A&O Shearman reportedly combines foundation models with curated data and proprietary legal expertise, deploys the resulting system internally, and commercialises it to corporate legal departments. Its forecast of hybrid lawyer-engineer roles also develops the cluster’s workforce-redesign theme, although it does not establish comparative quality or long-term commercial durability.
qs: Contract Matrix combines advanced prompt engineering with curated data lakes and proprietary expertise, enabling AI to deliver outputs that sound like the work of highly specialized lawyers.
Contract Matrix is now widely adopted at the firm and even being sold to corporate councils with Microsoft  -  Wakeling believes that GenAI will have big implications for talent.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s significance lies in redesigning legal-service delivery rather than merely procuring a tool, and materially extends the cluster with a concrete incumbent-firm model: combining foundation models with curated data and proprietary expertise, then commercialising the resulting contract system to corporate legal departments. Its forecast of hybrid legal-engineering roles also reinforces the cluster’s workforce-composition theme. It does not, however, quantify buyer savings, pricing effects, or productivity and accuracy gains.
qs: Contract Matrix combines advanced prompt engineering with curated data lakes and proprietary expertise, enabling AI to deliver outputs that sound like the work of highly specialized lawyers.
Contract Matrix is now widely adopted at the firm and even being sold to corporate councils with Microsoft  -  Wakeling believes that GenAI will have big implications for talent.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Wakeling accepts the case for redesigning legal delivery rather than merely adding off-the-shelf tools, and materially extends it with A&O Shearman’s operating model: multidisciplinary development, commercially screened software and advisory revenue, substantial implementation work, and continued junior hiring to avoid future succession gaps. His evidence remains qualitative and firm-specific, consistent with the cluster’s caution about market-wide conclusions.
qs: It was only when you built your own system, fully redesigned how you did the work that you were able to really take time out in a big way and actually get benefits.
Mistake if you, you do not have enough lawyers to serve your clients in five years ‘cause you managed for AI.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Wakeling materially extends the cluster’s non-zero-sum account by showing how a law firm can respond to stronger corporate AI buyers through paid software licensing, bespoke expertise-driven workflows and deployment advice. His reported bank workflow and profitable product offer concrete, though case-specific and self-reported, evidence that client savings and new law-firm revenue can coexist; they do not demonstrate broad insourcing or declining outside-counsel spend.
qs: They’re paying a per annum license fee for legal tech, AI, augmented from a law firm, and we entered into partnership with Microsoft to make that happen.

And so we devised the system with lots of expertise from from our regulatory knowledge, and then agreed with them a workflow that would achieve compliance and it was much cheaper than the human alternative.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts that AI is driving law-firm business-model and talent changes, and extends the cluster with a concrete example: A&O Shearman’s development and commercialization of a proprietary AI product, alongside a forecast of hybrid lawyer-engineer roles. It does not directly substantiate pyramid contraction, revenue loss or training-pipeline effects.
qs: We discussed how one of the world’s leading law firms is reshaping its business model around artificial intelligence.
He foresees lawyers working in hybrid roles—part legal expert, part engineer.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Wakeling accepts the need to rethink legal education and materially develops the cluster’s AI-readiness proposition with a concrete teaching model: students should decide whether AI is suitable, explain their prompting choices, and critically verify and correct outputs. His evidence of adoption and prediction of wider uptake remain observational and explicitly early-stage; he does not address lifelong development or who should fund apprenticeship.
qs: What they’re doing is they’re forcing those students to think, should I even use an AI system here?
And the third thing is that you’re still applying critical thinking and you are validating and taking the best and fixing the worst of the AI output.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Wakeling accepts that legal-specific products can create differentiated value, but materially sharpens the proposition by making defensibility conditional on task-level ROI and selective investment. His experience suggests that specialist lawyer–engineer development may justify its cost for scalable, high-value products, whereas basic extraction is readily commoditised and offers little margin.
qs: And then the Harvey fine tuning was when we’re really going big for something which we think could be industry utility scale, maybe other law firms wanna license that it, it’s so good.
It became clear to us after a period of time, there was no margin in that.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-reconfiguration framing and adds a concrete firm-level case: modest initial efficiencies led to a firm-specific system built on foundation models, broad deployment and emerging legal-technical roles. Its emphasis on validation and selecting appropriate use cases also aligns with capability-dependent adoption, although it provides little evidence on verification burdens or apprenticeship risks.
qs: Early applications were modest, saving small increments of time, but they proved adoption the technology could work for legal use cases  -  From there, the firm developed Contract Matrix, an in-house system layered on top of foundation models like OpenAI’s.
He even said that law schools are already training students to think in terms of prompt engineering, validation, and spotting the right use cases for applying AI tools  -

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts AI as an operating-model and business-model transformation, then materially extends the cluster with a concrete incumbent-firm example: A&O Shearman combines foundation models with proprietary data and expertise, commercialises the resulting system to corporate legal departments, and anticipates hybrid legal–engineering roles. This strengthens the cluster’s claims about differentiated delivery architectures and talent redesign, while offering adoption claims rather than independently measured returns.
qs: We discussed how one of the world’s leading law firms is reshaping its business model around artificial intelligence.
Contract Matrix combines advanced prompt engineering with curated data lakes and proprietary expertise, enabling AI to deliver outputs that sound like the work of highly specialized lawyers.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim and materially extends it with a concrete law-firm production model: proprietary expertise and curated data are embedded into an AI product, lawyers test and configure the system, hybrid legal-technical roles emerge, and the firm experiments with commercial products and advisory services. Its caution against anticipatory staffing cuts and lack of quantified outcomes also align with the cluster’s uncertainty about labour and sector-wide productivity effects.
qs: Contract Matrix combines advanced prompt engineering with curated data lakes and proprietary expertise, enabling AI to deliver outputs that sound like the work of highly specialized lawyers.
Our objective is to explore the future business model for a law firm.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Wakeling accepts that AI will augment and reorganise legal-service production rather than simply eliminate lawyers. He materially extends the cluster with A&O Shearman’s operating model: multidisciplinary implementation teams, specialist knowledge layered onto foundation models, commercially disciplined product development, fixed-fee incentives and SaaS revenue, alongside continued junior hiring and a shift toward hybrid legal-technical skills.
qs: So my job in the firm and I run a team of lawyers, developers, and data scientists to do this, is to explore that future business model, which is augmented by AI.
So I think it’s gonna be not stark, it’s gonna be a changing skillset, which might, not mean fewer people frankly, but different kinds of people.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Wakeling accepts the cluster’s framing of legal AI as workflow and service redesign rather than an off-the-shelf software purchase. He materially develops it by tying customisation and subject-matter expertise to commercial discipline: firms should invest deeply, redesign work, test client demand and terminate projects that cannot produce client value and law-firm profitability.
qs: And it is not just taking software out of the box that’s probably not gonna do what you want.
We’re trying to really drive a good business that produces a good return for our clients and still is profitable for a law firm.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially develops it through A&O Shearman’s progression from modest AI efficiencies to proprietary product development and software sales, illustrating blurred boundaries between legal delivery and technology provision. Its prediction of hybrid legal–engineering roles also supports organisational redesign, though the evidence remains qualitative rather than a measured demonstration of value capture.
qs: Contract Matrix is now widely adopted at the firm and even being sold to corporate councils with Microsoft  -  Wakeling believes that GenAI will have big implications for talent.
He foresees lawyers working in hybrid roles—part legal expert, part engineer.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wakeling accepts the cluster’s core view that AI redesigns legal work rather than simply replacing lawyers, and materially extends it with firm-level evidence: effective systems require substantial lawyer expertise, testing and lawyer–data-scientist collaboration; deployment choices should vary with cost, scalability and expected return; and junior roles may shift toward new technical capabilities rather than disappear. His warning about automation of commoditised tasks and investment barriers for smaller firms reinforces the cluster’s selective, operating-model-focused framing.
qs: I mentioned Richard, about how you have to invest a lot of elbow grease to get that subject matter expertise into the system.
So I think it’s gonna be not stark, it’s gonna be a changing skillset, which might, not mean fewer people frankly, but different kinds of people.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Wakeling supports the cluster’s core concern that firms risk damaging the future expertise pipeline if they cut junior recruitment in anticipation of automation. He notes that developing productive lawyers takes years and warns that premature reductions could leave firms unable to meet later client demand, while also observing that AI creates new junior work in system development and testing. He does not substantially address the cluster’s proposed reconstruction of apprenticeship through simulation and deliberate independent practice.
qs: But, and there are two very difficult things business challenges for a law firm or someone investing in a law firm when looking at this, the first one is it takes five years to get a very junior person into someone very productive.
Mistake if you, you do not have enough lawyers to serve your clients in five years ‘cause you managed for AI.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Wakeling supports the synthesis’s central view that AI is more likely to reshape legal roles and skills than eliminate lawyers wholesale. His continued junior hiring, emphasis on system-building and verification, and warning against cutting future capacity also align with the finding that broad displacement is not yet established, although his evidence is firm-specific rather than sector-wide.
qs: So I think it’s gonna be not stark, it’s gonna be a changing skillset, which might, not mean fewer people frankly, but different kinds of people.
And our juniors in my group, I’m still hiring junior lawyers, and they’re very busy and that’s what they’re doing.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Wakeling accepts the cluster’s core complementarity proposition: AI changes the tasks and skills required of lawyers without necessarily reducing headcount. His team’s continued junior hiring and AI-development work support caution against pre-emptive staffing cuts, while his smaller-firm investment concern is consistent with possible restructuring rather than inevitable profession-wide displacement.
qs: And our juniors in my group, I’m still hiring junior lawyers, and they’re very busy and that’s what they’re doing.
So I think it’s gonna be not stark, it’s gonna be a changing skillset, which might, not mean fewer people frankly, but different kinds of people.

kp.k: Early deployment produced anecdotal rather than measured efficiency evidence
kp.d: Wakeling says the firm was the first globally to roll out generative AI, partnering with Harvey and reaching 4,000 people by Christmas 2022 under information-security safeguards and guardrails. He describes meaningful but modest initial benefits, including overcoming writer’s block, while explicitly acknowledging that time-saving evidence was anecdotal rather than strong statistical data. This prompted development of products with clearer business propositions and return-on-investment comparisons.
qs: By Christmas 2022, we had 4,000 people, and we all kept it a giant secret in the firm.
our method of understanding the difference it was making to lawyers’ days was quite anecdotal
It wasn’t the best statistical data, so we then started building on products, which were much clearer on the proposition for the business and a return investment.

kp.k: Contract Matrix encodes specialist expertise above underlying models
kp.d: Wakeling describes Contract Matrix as a firm-built overlay on foundation and specialist models, using extensive contextual prompts and curated specialist databases mainly through retrieval augmented generation. A single finance-contract question can require two or three A4 sides of context, including examples and market practice. He claims this enables highly specialised legal outputs, including with GPT-5 at the interview date; the interview supplies no independent performance measurements.
qs: We built it as an overlay on top of foundation models and specialist models like Harvey.
We might have two or three A4 sides, which give context to what the question is, what good looks like, what bad looks like.
The second thing it’s doing is curating very good data lakes. We use it mainly for RAG.

kp.k: Fixed fees align automation incentives with preserved margins
kp.d: Wakeling identifies complex but repetitive work already priced at fixed fees or under intense price pressure as particularly suitable for adoption. Lawyers invest upfront in encoding methods and expertise, then offer faster delivery while continuing to stand behind outcomes. His proposed economics shift from selling hours toward maintaining software-based intellectual property and scaling across clients, conditional on sufficient demand and preserved margins.
qs: It’s complex, but it’s still repetitive and it is either already done at a fixed fee.
I will still stand behind the outcome.
So I can preserve margin as long as we can preserve margin, incentives are right.
They are instead curating that IP in the software. And that is a fundamental economics of a software product, right, is hours spent is irrelevant. You are going for scale.

kp.k: Specialist fine-tuning requires exceptional investment and prospective scale
kp.d: Wakeling distinguishes routine Contract Matrix prompt engineering and retrieval from unusual, expensive work with Harvey involving fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. He describes one of four modules developed with Harvey: a merger-control and foreign-direct-investment workflow ingesting transaction financials, identifying filing jurisdictions and requesting additional information through the deal. Such investment is justified prospectively by potential industry-utility scale and licensing to other firms, not claimed as an easily scalable development method.
qs: We don’t do fine tuning as a matter of course, but when we do it, we’ve done it directly with Harvey.
With Harvey we start developing four modules.
it will tell the user which jurisdictions are gonna trigger merger approvals or antitrust filings, and which won’t, and those where more information is needed.
And they did reinforcement learning directly with the data scientists at Harvey. So that is very unusual, but we can’t scale that. It’s very expensive, right?

kp.k: Commoditised extraction failed commercially, prompting a specialist pivot
kp.d: Wakeling reports that straightforward data extraction, simple discovery and basic M&A due-diligence interrogation proved unprofitable because many competitors offered them. His expectation that GPT-5 or 6 could perform such work rapidly is a prediction, distinct from the reported margin failure. The group consequently redirected resources toward differentiated subject-matter expertise and made that differentiation a threshold for new AI investment.
qs: It became clear to us after a period of time, there was no margin in that. Everyone was doing it.
Probably GPT-5 or 6 will do it in 30 seconds with, a prompt by someone who has a college degree.
We couldn’t quite make it profitable, so we pivoted away from that.
And if we don’t have something in the firm, which is a little bit special, and you couldn’t find in lots of other places, then we’re not doing that project.

kp.k: Software licensing creates a distinct law-firm revenue stream
kp.d: Wakeling reports annual SaaS licensing of Contract Matrix without the firm’s specialist expertise baked in, principally to corporate counsel and also some small law firms. Microsoft supplies workflow integration, scale and robust business-to-business deployment, with Harvey contributing AI components. He says the product makes money and attributes its appeal partly to lawyers’ established Microsoft Word workflows; reluctance by large premium firms to license from a rival is his interpretation, not a measured market finding.
qs: So Contract Matrix without all of this expertise baked into it.
They’re paying a per annum license fee for legal tech, AI, augmented from a law firm, and we entered into partnership with Microsoft to make that happen.
Harvey is also in that partnership for some of the AI pieces.
Yeah, to corporate counsels. There are a few small law firms who will license it.

kp.k: Custom workflows and AI advisory extend monetisation beyond SaaS
kp.d: The other two revenue categories Wakeling identifies are bespoke expertise-rich workflows atop Contract Matrix and advice on deploying AI beyond clients’ legal functions. He cites a system for a top three US global bank intended to demonstrate compliance to European regulators, claiming it was much cheaper than the human alternative without quantifying savings. The advisory work addresses adoption, hallucinations, intellectual-property infringement and regulatory risk, combining relatively traditional legal advice with deployment experience.
qs: we recently did a system for a top three US bank, global bank
then agreed with them a workflow that would achieve compliance and it was much cheaper than the human alternative.
we are getting asked by lots of clients to advise on how to deploy AI in their businesses outside legal space.
It’s strategic, it’s writing opinions, it’s forming views on like proper risk mitigation, but it’s informed by all that tech expertise I just described.

kp.k: Software-intensive firms may gain economies-of-scale advantages
kp.d: Wakeling observes large firms hiring developers and expects that trend to continue. Drawing an explicit analogy with banks’ software-intensive evolution over 20–30 years, he suggests law firms could become technology-oriented organisations while retaining substantial human workforces. He also speculates that the cost and difficulty of AI investment could cause legal-sector rationalisation and disadvantage smaller firms. These are prospective structural arguments, not documented consolidation outcomes or a specified new staffing shape.
qs: very big law firms who have the scale, ‘cause I think this is an economies of scale business. They’re already hiring developers to look at products.
There’s a huge number of bankers, but they are augmented everywhere by systems, data analytics, compliance tools, whatever it is.
There might be some rationalization in the legal sector though, because I wonder if it’s too expensive and hard to invest in AI for smaller firms.

kp.k: Long training cycles counsel caution about cutting junior recruitment
kp.d: Although Wakeling predicts complete displacement of some jobs, he warns that a five-year development cycle makes reducing junior intake on anticipated AI savings commercially risky. He reports continuing demand and ongoing junior hiring in his group, where encoding expertise and testing systems create substantial work. His qualified expectation is a changing skill mix that might not entail fewer people, rather than a definite reduction in headcount or leverage.
qs: I think also that some jobs will be completely displaced.
it takes five years to get a very junior person into someone very productive.
That is a very, very brutal. Mistake if you, you do not have enough lawyers to serve your clients in five years ‘cause you managed for AI.
And our juniors in my group, I’m still hiring junior lawyers, and they’re very busy and that’s what they’re doing.
it’s gonna be a changing skillset, which might, not mean fewer people frankly, but different kinds of people.

kp.k: Hybrid legal skills combine expertise, prompting and data collaboration
kp.d: Wakeling describes lawyers in his team developing expertise in legal prompt engineering, curating data lakes and collaborating substantively with data scientists. This is his account of current role development; the interviewer’s characterisation of future lawyers as part lawyer, part engineer summarises that direction but is not evidence that all lawyers already occupy such roles.
qs: I’ve got a load of lawyers in my team who are brilliant at prompt engineering for legal tasks.
They understand how to curate data lakes.
They can hold their own in a conversation with someone who is a data scientist, and they’ll have a good exchange and then the lawyer will take something away and the data scientist will.

kp.k: Legal education should teach tool selection and human verification
kp.d: Drawing on observations and conversations with UK, European and US institutions, Wakeling reports emerging teaching that asks students whether AI is suitable, how to construct prompts and how to check and correct outputs. He endorses recognising when no tool is fit for purpose and preserving critical thinking, including checking fabricated case law. He describes this as early-stage practice and predicts wider normalisation over the next few years, rather than presenting a systematic survey of legal education.
qs: I want you to tell me your prompts, why you’ve crafted them the way you have.
I want you to tell me how to validate those prompts and make sure they don’t have mistakes or hallucinations or make up case law or whatever the risks are of the system.
Because it’s a very good answer if you say there isn’t one fit for purpose.
you’re still applying critical thinking and you are validating and taking the best and fixing the worst of the AI output.
I would think that’ll be par for the course over the next few years.

kp.k: Commercial transformation requires incentives, redesign and failure tolerance
kp.d: Wakeling recommends aligning incentives around relief from repetitive tasks and payment for system architecture and expertise, then letting successful adopters persuade colleagues. He rejects demonstration-led 'innovation theater' and argues for terminating projects lacking a commercially viable business model. He stresses substantial implementation work, possible misjudgments of client demand or lawyer workflows, and portfolio-level acceptance of failure rather than expecting out-of-the-box software to deliver transformation.
qs: Find the incentives for adoption
get those people to talk to their friends about it and really give them the platform to communicate with everyone else.
It has to be about exploring that commercially viable future business model. If it’s not about that, then you probably want to kill whatever the AI project is.
In my experience, to get the AI systems to really perform, you have to invest enormous amounts of work.
Just on a portfolio basis, you need to win a lot more than you lose there.

kp.k: Adoption remains incomplete despite early deployment
kp.d: Wakeling endorses the technology-sector adoption-curve framework based on his experience and recommends learning from established change-management approaches in other sectors. He says his firm has progressed through the early majority but still faces the late majority, with laggards not yet addressed. This qualifies broad rollout claims: access and initial deployment do not mean working-practice change is complete.
qs: I’ve done the early majority of my firm. I now need to crack the late majority
And the laggards I haven’t even started thinking about yet.
there is a genuine adoption curve and it takes time and it’s a hard job.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: David Wakeling describes a progression from modest time savings with broadly deployed legal AI to more specialised, commercially targeted workflow tools.
pts.d: Wakeling says the firm rolled out Harvey to 4,000 people by Christmas 2022 in an information-security-compliant environment with guardrails, claiming it was the first law firm globally to deploy generative AI. Initial benefits included overcoming writer’s block and saving small amounts of time. He explicitly describes the evidence for those savings as anecdotal. Contract Matrix was subsequently developed to compare conventional human tasks against AI-augmented work more clearly and incorporate specialist legal expertise through extensive prompts and curated databases, principally using retrieval-augmented generation. His claim is that this additional layer can produce highly specialised legal outputs; the interview supplies no quantified accuracy or productivity comparison.

pts.k: Wakeling argues that AI can shift repetitive specialist work toward fixed-fee, software-supported delivery, preserving margins while reducing lawyers’ hours.
pts.d: He locates the clearest incentive alignment in complex but repetitive work that is already fixed-fee or under severe price pressure. Lawyers invest time upfront in encoding methods, knowledge and market practice into software, then seek to deliver the same work faster while continuing to stand behind the outcome. The commercial proposition is conditional: the investment must generate client demand and sufficient repeat sales. The resulting economics depend less on hours worked and more on serving additional clients with limited incremental effort. This is an account of an intended and pursued business model, not evidence that all hourly legal work will disappear.

pts.k: Wakeling says advanced specialist workflows can support new legal products, but bespoke model development is expensive and needs a sufficiently large commercial opportunity.
pts.d: He describes working with Harvey on four modules, including a merger-control and foreign-direct-investment workflow that ingests transaction financial information, consults the firm’s legal databases, identifies jurisdictions potentially requiring filings, requests missing information and supports the user during a deal. According to Wakeling, antitrust lawyers worked directly with Harvey data scientists using reinforcement learning because Contract Matrix was not suitable for that workflow. He sees Contract Matrix as a lower-barrier approach and bespoke tuning as appropriate for potentially industry-scale utilities, possibly licensed by other law firms. The possibility of broader licensing is prospective rather than an established result in this example.

pts.k: Wakeling claims that basic extraction and discovery work is becoming commoditised, while distinctive legal expertise offers a stronger basis for profitable AI products.
pts.d: He reports that the firm could not make a workstream involving straightforward extraction, simple discovery and basic M&A due-diligence interrogation profitable because competitors offered similar capabilities. He speculates that GPT-5 or GPT-6 could perform such work in 30 seconds with a prompt from a college graduate. That speed statement is a prediction, not a reported test. The experience led his group to redirect resources toward specialist expertise and to reject new projects unless the firm possesses something sufficiently distinctive.

pts.k: Wakeling identifies three AI-related revenue streams: software licensing, customised specialist workflows and advice on clients’ AI deployment.
pts.d: He reports annual SaaS licensing of Contract Matrix, without the firm’s full specialist expertise included, mainly to corporate counsel and also to some small law firms, through a partnership involving Microsoft and Harvey. He says this product makes money and attributes its suitability partly to integration with lawyers’ Microsoft Word-based practices and Microsoft’s deployment scale. A second stream adds customised legal expertise: he cites a regulatory-compliance workflow for a top-three US bank as much cheaper than the human alternative, without supplying figures. A third involves advising clients outside legal services on AI adoption and risks, informed by the firm’s implementation experience. He predicts that large premium competitors will be slower to license its software, partly because of pride.

pts.k: Wakeling predicts increasingly software-oriented law firms and changing legal skills, with some job displacement but not necessarily fewer lawyers overall.
pts.d: He says large law firms are already hiring developers and expects that trend to continue. Drawing an analogy with banks, he suggests firms could become much more technology-oriented while retaining substantial professional workforces. He predicts some complete job displacement but does not identify the jobs or quantify losses. Conversely, building and testing legal AI systems creates work for junior lawyers, including prompt engineering, database curation and collaboration with data scientists. He reports continued junior hiring in his own group. Although asked about the staffing pyramid, he does not predict a specific replacement shape.

pts.k: Wakeling suggests that training lead times constrain staffing reductions, while the costs of AI investment may disadvantage smaller firms.
pts.d: He says it takes about five years for a very junior lawyer to become highly productive, making aggressive hiring reductions risky if demand remains strong. His firm is busy and continues to need junior lawyers both for client work and system development. Separately, he characterises AI development as an economies-of-scale business and speculates that smaller firms may find investment too costly or difficult, potentially producing sector rationalisation. He does not specify whether that would mean mergers, exits or another market change.

pts.k: Wakeling expects AI-use judgment, prompt engineering and human verification to become normal elements of legal education over the next few years.
pts.d: Based on encounters with universities and conversations with leading law schools, he reports teaching that asks students whether AI is suitable for a legal problem, how they would construct prompts and how they would check and correct the results. The competence he advocates includes deciding not to use an unsuitable system, rather than assuming AI is always appropriate. His prediction concerns educational practice and hybrid legal-technical skills, not autonomous reliance on AI output.

pts.k: Wakeling argues that commercially meaningful AI adoption requires aligned incentives, extensive implementation work and acceptance of failure, rather than demonstrations or out-of-the-box software alone.
pts.d: He recommends connecting adoption to relief from repetitive work and viable fixed-fee delivery, then enabling successful practitioners to encourage colleagues. He argues that distinctive specialist systems require substantial effort and commercial risk because demand or workflow assumptions can prove wrong. His firm has reached what he calls the early majority, while the late majority and laggards remain adoption challenges. He presents lessons from technology-sector adoption literature as applicable to law and other professional services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Wakeling’s first-hand implementation and commercial experience; forecasts rely on judgment and analogy rather than systematic measurements.
pts.d: The interview, published by Richard Lichtenstein on 6 October 2025, attributes these substantive claims to Wakeling as the partner leading A&O Shearman’s AI group. Concrete examples include the reported 4,000-person deployment, the abandoned extraction workstream, specialist development with Harvey, client SaaS licensing, the bank compliance workflow and continued junior hiring. Wakeling explicitly qualifies the initial productivity evidence as anecdotal. No benchmark scores, measured hallucination rates, independently verified financial results, detailed cost comparisons or sector-wide employment data are provided. The banking analogy supports his organisational forecast; university conversations support his education account; adoption books and personal experience support his change-management claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes a 2022 initial rollout, current 2025 products and hiring, near-term education changes, and less precisely timed market and employment predictions.
pts.d: The Harvey rollout is dated to Christmas 2022. The specialist Harvey workflows were launched at the beginning of the interview year, implicitly 2025; licensing, custom development and junior recruitment are described as current. Educational changes are expected to become normal over the next few years. Five years is the stated lawyer-development horizon, not a deadline for replacement. Job displacement, technology-oriented firms and possible sector rationalisation have no firm dates. Profitability depends on distinctive expertise, repeatable delivery, suitable fees, sufficient demand and substantial upfront work. Bespoke tuning is qualified by high costs; adoption remains incomplete. The GPT-5-or-6 extraction prediction is model-linked and speculative, not a dated performance finding.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern premium law firms, specialist and junior lawyers, smaller firms, corporate legal buyers and legal educators.
pts.d: Large firms may gain software-related revenues and employ more developers and data scientists. Specialist lawyers can encode expertise into reusable systems and potentially reduce repetitive hours while preserving fixed-fee margins. Juniors face changing skills and some unspecified displacement risk, but also system-building work and continued demand. Smaller firms are both potential software customers and potentially disadvantaged investors in proprietary AI. Corporate counsel buy SaaS; banks and other corporate clients commission tailored workflows or seek AI-risk advice. Other large premium firms are portrayed as reluctant licensees. Students and educators face new expectations concerning tool selection, prompting and verification. The source does not make concrete claims about access to justice, unmet civil legal need or public-facing autonomous legal advice.
